title: A Chain-of-Thought Prompting Approach with LLMs for Evaluating Students’ Formative Assessment Responses in Science
venue: The Thirty-Eighth AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence (AAAI-24)
extended_summary:
This paper addresses how large language models can be used to score and explain students’ open-ended formative assessment responses in K-12 science, a task that is difficult and time-consuming for teachers. The authors focus on middle school Earth Science short-answer assessments, where students must demonstrate conceptual understanding and scientific reasoning rather than produce highly structured answers. The study also examines whether chain-of-thought prompting and human-in-the-loop active learning can improve alignment between GPT-4 scoring and human scoring, while generating explanations that may be useful for feedback and rubric refinement.

The intervention studied is a GPT-4-based automated assessment pipeline that combines few-shot prompting, chain-of-thought reasoning, inter-rater-reliability-informed prompt construction, and one iteration of active learning. Human scorers first established consensus on a subset of responses, then these agreed examples and explanatory reasoning chains were inserted into prompts. The model was then used to score three formative assessment questions from the SPICE middle school Earth Science water runoff curriculum, and prompt examples were further refined based on observed model errors. The approach was evaluated against zero-shot, few-shot, and few-shot-with-CoT baselines using accuracy, macro F1, and quadratic weighted kappa.

The population consisted of 270 students from two Vanderbilt-approved SPICE studies at a public middle school in the Southeastern United States. The curriculum lasted three weeks and centered on redesigning a schoolyard to reduce water runoff under cost and accessibility constraints. The assessments targeted students’ conceptual understanding of water runoff and conservation of matter. Teachers are also part of the broader use context because the system is intended to support teacher scoring, feedback, and rubric revision, and the paper additionally references anecdotal teacher interview feedback about the usefulness of model-generated explanations.

The main conclusion is that GPT-4, combined with chain-of-thought prompting and active learning, can achieve strong and in several cases near-human agreement for scoring middle school science formative assessments, while also producing explanations linked to rubric criteria. However, performance varied by question and subscore, and the method was vulnerable to overfitting, especially for simpler subtasks or ambiguous rubric/question formulations. The authors conclude that human-in-the-loop use is important, both to correct model weaknesses and to improve rubrics and question design. They also note ethical concerns related to privacy, bias, and hallucinations, and frame the work as a promising but still limited step toward practical classroom use.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-family large language model chatbot used for natural language generation and analysis tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as GPT-4 in a human-in-the-loop chain-of-thought prompting plus active learning pipeline to score middle school Earth Science short-answer formative assessments and generate rubric-linked explanations/feedback.

findings.finding_summary: GPT-4 mostly aligned with human scorers on automated scoring of three middle school Earth Science formative assessment questions from SPICE. Across 11 subscores and total scores, 9 reached 'strong' agreement or better at some stage (QWK >= 0.8), 4 reached 'almost perfect' agreement (QWK > 0.9), and all but one subscore achieved Macro F1 >= 0.90 at some point in the evaluation pipeline. The dataset came from 270 students, though missing/non-consenting data reduced usable responses.
findings.measure: Automated scoring agreement with human raters using Macro F1, accuracy, and Cohen's Quadratic Weighted Kappa (QWK) across question subscores and total scores
findings.effect_size: QWK up to 1.00; Macro F1 up to 1.00 depending on subscore/implementation

findings.finding_summary: For Question 1 (Arrow Size), GPT-4 achieved moderate agreement even zero-shot (Acc=0.87, F1=0.84, QWK=0.68). With few-shot prompting, performance reached perfect test-set scoring (Acc=1.00, F1=1.00, QWK=1.00), while the full CoT+active learning approach achieved Acc=0.98, F1=0.97, QWK=0.95.
findings.measure: Test-set scoring performance for Q1 Arrow Size
findings.effect_size: Zero-shot QWK=0.68; Few-shot QWK=1.00; CoT+AL QWK=0.95

findings.finding_summary: For Question 2, the full CoT+active learning method improved overall total-score agreement to Acc=0.85, F1=0.79, QWK=0.87, outperforming the zero-shot baseline on QWK (0.65). However, some scientific reasoning subscores worsened as CoT and active learning were added; for example, Q2 Arrow Direction Reasoning declined to F1=0.65 and QWK=0.30 under CoT+AL, and the authors report overfitting on ambiguous responses.
findings.measure: Test-set scoring performance for Q2 subscores and total score
findings.effect_size: Q2 Total Score QWK=0.87 with CoT+AL; Q2 Arrow Direction Reasoning QWK=0.30 with CoT+AL

findings.finding_summary: For Question 3, the full method improved total-score agreement to Acc=0.81, F1=0.80, QWK=0.90. Some subscores achieved perfect agreement, including Q3 Arrow Size Reasoning with few-shot and with CoT+AL (Acc=1.00, F1=1.00, QWK=1.00), but Q3 Runoff Direction was overfit during active learning, dropping from QWK=0.84 with Few-Shot, CoT to 0.75 with CoT+AL.
findings.measure: Test-set scoring performance for Q3 subscores and total score
findings.effect_size: Q3 Total Score QWK=0.90; Q3 Arrow Size Reasoning QWK=1.00; Q3 Runoff Direction QWK fell to 0.75 after CoT+AL

findings.finding_summary: In a disagreement analysis, the lead author reviewed 22 human-model scoring disagreements and agreed with the model in 3 cases (1 conceptual, 2 reasoning), suggesting some model judgments may surface rubric or human-scoring issues. The authors also found that CoT and active learning could overfit, with errors tied to keyword sensitivity, reused evidence across subscores, and inconsistent adherence to provided reasoning patterns.
findings.measure: Qualitative review of human-model scoring disagreements and error patterns

quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical evaluation of a specific tool use case, but it is not an RCT or QED on student learning outcomes. The study mainly assesses agreement with human scoring using held-out test data and qualitative error analysis.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows promising but mixed operational gains in automated assessment accuracy and explanation generation, with high agreement on several subscores but overfitting and weaker performance on some reasoning items. Impacts are substantial for scoring alignment in places, but they are task-specific and not linked to direct student outcome effects.
